translations.text: Commentary: What is the renunciation and hatred of nature? This is what this holy father is saying:
for God at first created our nature free of passion and pure, and gave us the power of thought, so that we might think on what is good and on virtue;
and the power of anger, so that we might be wrathful against the demons and the passions;
and the power of desire, so that we might have desire and longing for the kingdom of heaven. But we changed these powers through sin, and acquired desire for filthy things,
and anger against our brothers, and the thinking of wickedness; and we changed those good workings of our nature into evil, and made passion into our nature.

Now therefore, whoever has driven out such passions as these, planted within us through our negligence, and has become victorious over them, that person has truly hated and renounced that passion-ridden nature;
and this is the true departure from the world: the renunciation of that passion-ridden nature, and going out to seek that first, passionless nature which God gave us.
Commentary. The passions of the soul are these: vainglory, pride, wrath, grief, despondency, hatreds and others;
such as these. And the passions of the flesh are: gluttony, love of silver, fornication, love of the affairs of the world.
Those, then, who are overcome by the passions of the soul need a discerning guide, who may give them a little bodily comfort,
so that they may not grow proud as people who fast and are zealous; and in this way, sometimes with fasting and sometimes with rest,
he may heal their illnesses with discernment. Such people are like those who came out of Egypt, whom Moses led.
But those who are overcome by the passions of the flesh need as a guide a man whose life is almost like that of the bodiless angels, through fasting and severity and mercilessness toward the flesh.
And they are like those who came out of Sodom; for Father John has taken Egypt as a figure of the passions of the soul, and Sodom of those of the flesh.

Commentary. How is it hard and narrow and light? In this way: it is hard because of the guarding of the senses, the guarding of which is hard for those who have become accustomed to letting them loose.
And it is narrow because of ascetic labors and the humbling of the flesh, and because of the cutting off of those long-standing habits.
And it is light because of hope in God and because of the eternal good things.
The [?] of the field is a figure of the severity of the virtues.
Commentary. Fear is twofold: one kind belongs to beginners and one to the perfect.
In this place this great father is speaking of that of the beginners; for when a man is in sins and becomes afraid lest death overtake him in sin,
and for this reason goes out from the world, so as not to fall into those same former evils, and labors with good ascetic labor;

and when that fear fades a little, because such people are not firm, he then becomes negligent again and resembles incense that has dissipated, for he began with ascetic labor and has come to negligence.
Commentary. Those who build with mud brick upon stones are those who have gone out from the world without entering into obedience, and have begun to build very great virtues;
and because they had no guide, they grew weak and could not complete their foundation; rather, they began very great deeds and arrived at negligence.

As for those who set up pillars on the sand, he means those who withdrew from the world and took up a life of separation; and since they did not have the foundation of obedience, for this reason they could not make good progress.
But those who ran on foot and grew warm, he means those who entered the good racecourse of obedience and made good progress.
Commentary. I think he says this about such people as have been banished by the king and exiled from their homelands for some offense,
and the king would go to the country where they had been exiled.
And one of them would be denounced to the king, as though he were plotting some evil against him. Then the king would order him to be brought before him against his will.
But when they brought him, he would examine him and find no fault in him, and he would recall him from exile, honor him, and seat him at his own table.
-- So he took this as a figure of such a thing: an involuntary departure from the world, on account of some affliction, since many times even that turns out well.

Commentary. By "faces" he means the powers of the soul and the deeds of the soul, for it is from the outward appearances and from the [?] of a person's actions that our enemies the demons learn the thoughts of the heart;
otherwise they know nothing of our mind by themselves. For they sow their own wickedness in our soul and wait to learn in what way we have received
their seed, and from our deeds and conduct they learn how we have received it.
Commentary. Death is twofold, visible and invisible: for there is the dead person who has died bodily, and there is the dead person who has died in soul, because he has not set out toward life.

Commentary. False ascetic struggle is this: when a person struggles for the praise of men. But true struggle is that which is done for God's sake and by the word of the fathers, in keeping with him who says:
"I do nothing of myself." That which is done by the counsel of the fathers is both perfect and kept free from pride.
Commentary. This comes about from negligence and lack of vigilance, from loftiness and self-esteem, and by God's permission, so that we may be instructed and humbled.
Commentary. The impurity of the world is love of pleasures, love of material goods, and love of glory.
Commentary. A harbor for ships, understood spiritually, brings life, but it can also bring drowning. Yet it is not the harbor that causes the drowning, but the negligence of those who are in it.
But whoever is diligent will find life and not drowning.
Commentary. What are the things that oppose the thought of our heart, if not material goods, possessions, foods, wills, luxuries, and passions?
Commentary. Exile from one's homeland becomes a cause of vainglory when a person presents himself as a child of great people and is presumptuous and arrogant.
Commentary. By separation from all things he means separation from thoughts and wills, for if these remain with a person, that exile is without profit.
Commentary. By "one's own" he means wills, and by "foreign" he means outward things, such as foods, kinsfolk, friends, and other such things.
Commentary. See how he condemns even mere thought and desires, for they were punished not for turning to the deed, but only for the desire,
For the people did not go down to Egypt in the flesh; they only conceived the desire to go there, and for this they were condemned never to enter the land of promise.
For this reason this blessed father John warns us to guard ourselves against evil desires.
Interpretation: He speaks of our relatives as "ours" because of our fleshly kinship, but as not ours because they do not speak what is better for our soul.
And again, the evil thoughts of the heart are also ours and not ours: ours because they are within us, but not ours because they come from the demons.
He takes Egypt as a figure of this world, which is full of the darkness of the passions.
Interpretation. How can he say that without obedience no one may see the Lord?
And how then did Mary of Egypt and Father Anthony and many others see him? But let us understand this saying as follows:
that whoever becomes so fervent and subjects the flesh to the spirit, and makes the reproof of conscience, which is the mind that reproves evil, the judge of himself,
and in whom is kindled the fierce fire of the love of God, that fire which has made him obedient to the divine commandments,
has attained that invisible obedience before visible obedience. As for those saints, then, who made progress without obedience,
since they acquired such a divine fire, for this reason they became what they were; but such a thing is hard and difficult to find,
and whoever has not acquired such a disposition of heart and such deeds will not see the face of God without obedience.
For a person must either become obedient to the commandments of God and reach such a measure, or acquire obedience to a spiritual teacher,
and through it attain obedience to God. And obedience to the teacher is itself obedience to God, for the one who obeys the teacher obeys for the sake of God's commandment.
Interpretation. The humble person is never confident that "I obey well," nor that "I have found forgiveness of sins"; and such a person has truly found forgiveness.
But whoever is proud is disobedient, and thinks that he obeys well and has found forgiveness of sins; yet such a person has by no means found forgiveness.
Interpretation. He is speaking of scrutinizing: when a disciple scrutinizes the words of the teacher, asking, "Why did he say this to me?" or "Why did he say that other thing?"
Interpretation. What was that error, if not eating in secret? For he had eaten something from the mules' load, and he confessed it,
and it does not mean fornication, as certain foolish people have imagined; otherwise how could that teacher have spoken about fornication with a smile?
Interpretation. He means disobedience and pride.
Interpretation. Obedience is the beginning of humility, for whoever does not recognize that he himself is lacking in virtues
cannot obey another; and so the knowledge of one's own weakness brings the soul to obedience.
And obedience gripped by the fear of God gives birth to humility, and humility drives out haughtiness. And in this way such a person becomes a house of dispassion.
Miriam the sister of Moses.
Interpretation. He says this about those who live in communities: that if you are humble, do spiritual works within your heart, and do not show it either by word or by outward appearance.
By "work" he means the prayer implanted in the mind. If, then, you were an accuser of others who were negligent, it is better that you not have those works at all,
and not accuse the brothers, but rather be like them than be arrogant and puffed up over those small works of yours.
Interpretation: He says this, that he was honored in the flesh and became despised in the spirit, for he did not care for his soul.
Interpretation: He who every day examines himself and judges himself, and whose life is spent in pain and care,
and who considers how that day and night have passed, he is a good merchant of his own works.
"Khada" (he called): he summoned.
It is the shame of prayer, for when we say, "Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors,"
then the remembrance of wrongs is the shame of that prayer of ours.
For this reason it is among the parents, for arrogant anger gives birth to the remembrance of wrongs, and the remembrance of wrongs gives birth to envy and murder.
"Khartuki", "khratuki": it is a hook in the middle of a pole [?]; they fasten it to the nose and two men drag it along.
For the days of fierce warfare are shortened by the power of the Holy Spirit.
Outside of nature are sodomy and falling with beasts; and to these he also added falling by the hand.
"Mine" for this reason, that they are joined to the soul; but "not mine", because they are fighters against the soul.
Humility is reckoning oneself lower than all, and this comes about through courage of mind and from the fear of God;
and it also comes about from falls, whose mother is pride.
For heresy is a perversion of the mind and a work of the tongue, but fornication changes all the senses of the body and the powers of the soul from being into non-being,
and it corrupts the image of God that is upon us.
"Remember him": he means that brother who carried his mother across the water.
He means the apostle Peter.
Immaterial are an angel, a demon and the soul; but the body is material.
By "light" he means gentleness, and by "sun" humility.
He set the bow as a figure for humility, on account of its many-colored good things and graces.
By "land" he means that of the Red Sea, which Moses revealed, and likewise Joshua at the Jordan.
The "one day" is that on which Noah came out of the ark.
By "natural" he means bodily things: noble birth, dexterity, being well educated, a good voice, beauty, and fineness of stature.
That is to say, whoever enters the monastic life with humility like that of Christ,
he will enter well and will go out from this transitory life, and will find pasture, that is, the divine rest.
These three are: gluttony, love of money, and vain pride. But whoever overcomes these three: gluttony by fasting;
vain pride by humility; love of money by hope in God and by prayer;
he has also overcome the other five, which are fornication, anger, sorrow, listlessness, and arrogance.
Negligence, listlessness, and lust are the night and darkness of the soul.
He says this of Paul the Apostle, who called a curse upon himself for the sake of his brethren.
From the sky a pillar of cloud comes down upon the sea and takes up water, and this is called a siphon.
The teachings for those newly entered are these: obedience, fasting, patience, fortitude of soul, not loving kin and possessions, humility, and prayer.
For those in the middle: long-suffering, gentleness, goodness, mercy, freedom from rancor, poverty [?], fasting, reverence, and prayer. And for the perfect:
love, joy, peace, discernment, and unerring understanding at every time and place and in every matter.
There are three passions: love of pleasure, love of money, and arrogance.
The eight thoughts are these: gluttony, fornication, love of money, anger, sorrow, listlessness, vainglory, and arrogance.
Three are the chief ones: gluttony, love of money, and pride. And the five are: fornication, anger, sorrow, listlessness, and arrogance.
The mind is itself the place and faculty of thinking, which is like the eye of the soul. A thought is a thing conceived and formed by the mind.
Guarding the mind means that a person keeps it entirely unreceptive even to the smallest approaches and thoughts that are not good.
Watching over thoughts means turning away a matter that one did not think up and that has come into the mind.
The distinction between these is of two kinds, for in one way the former is lower, and in the other way the latter.
Commentary. Every transgression of a commandment is called sin; idleness is not striving and not doing the works of God; and negligence is
when a person does good, but laxly and not fully; and passion is a settled inclination of our mind, afflicted and hard to drive out;
but a fall is falling into unbelief or into one of the bodily sins.
The soul is immaterial and the body is material, and for this reason the body is opposed to the soul.
That is to say, when one who is weak in spirit acquires patience in illnesses and trials, then let him understand that God has looked upon him with care.
By departure it speaks here of the time of death. But what does it mean when it says, "with one part," either "I go up" or "I go down"?
It speaks of the soul, for it is the soul that either goes up to heaven or goes down to the underworld, and does not stay in between; but the body remains on the earth.
He is speaking of the soul and the body of man, for the soul of man has received its being in the body,
and has been created in it. And this blessed one marvels at this: how, when it is separated from that in which it was created, it remains whole and unharmed and wholly unchanged.
By "fearful" he means the lover of the flesh, saying that whoever is fearful and faint-hearted, and pities his own flesh and loves it, let such a one not enter upon the ascetic struggle.
By "fall" he means bodily sin, and by "error" the soul's despair.
And he said that it is worse than the first fall because whoever has once made a vow of spiritual life and falls again finds it harder to rise, for he has fallen from a height.
And by the last "error" he means despair: those who fall into it perish, unless they have someone to raise them up.
What is the "mixed will" of which this blessed one speaks? It may be this: that often a man does some deed, and the will of God is in it,
and then immediately the will of the devil also becomes mixed with it, and the deed in turn becomes not good; and then the divine will also joins in it, and it becomes good.
He says this because fear leads a man to action, and love leads him to contemplation; and then those contemplations of love have no end, and thus comes about the going from strength to strength.
And may the Lord guard the entering in of fear, which enters into action, and the going out of love, which goes out to contemplation.
By "sudden fall" he means improprieties committed when one is carried away, whether in deed or in word, so that a man may not cut off hope
when some such thing befalls him; rather, even if he falls, let him struggle again and rise up and fight his enemies as though he had not fallen.
And such a one will be glorified by the angels, like that brother who fell into fornication and was not overcome by despair,
on whose account it was also revealed to an elder that this brother, after his fall, had conquered the enemies.
Christ, who remained three nights in the tomb, lives forever; and whoever conquers during three periods of time will die no more.
The three periods are childhood, youth and old age. Whoever conquers that passion during these three periods, death of the soul through spiritual sin will no longer befall him.
Although not always, yet often regret is a dissolver of good things. For when we are doing some good thing and regret it,
and think up something else, and become grieved, asking why we did not do that instead, then we scatter the good we have gathered. Let us understand this in the case of those
who are advancing in obedience and then regret it, asking why they did not take up solitary stillness, and who neglect obedience.
Then that regret brings about the dissolution of that good, until he has used up the good things he had acquired, and then he sees his own fall.
Thus I think he is speaking of the conscience.
This blessed one says that living alone is a hard thing, for one who lives with others, if he stumbles, has help from people;
but one who has withdrawn needs great caution so that he may not fall; rather, let him always entreat the Lord and guard himself.
And then God, when he sees that he is such a one, will give him too an angel as a helper.
After these, as I suppose, comes the fall into carnal sin, or the loss of the mind and madness, for these are the offspring of pride, as blasphemy is too.
Those living in solitude are fought by love of fire [?], listlessness, grief, anger, and pride. But those living in community are fought by gluttony, fornication, and arrogance.
Commentary. He calls prayer the middle, for it is the midpoint between solitary stillness and the contemplation of God;
and this blessed father John says: When I was in the middle, which is prayer, I reached those in the middle, who are the angels, for they are in the middle between God and human beings,
and "they enlightened the thirsting one," that is, in the matters that I thirsted and longed to know, they enlightened me by their revelation;
"So I asked how he was before his visible appearance," that is, before the Incarnation, in what form Christ was.
-- But on this matter even that angel who was speaking to me was unable to give an account; for not even the angels know the form of the Godhead; "but neither did the ruler desire it";
By this he means that although I asked, the ruler, which is the mind, does not wish to know such a matter,
And he says, "And how is he now?", that is, when he could not explain that first question to me, I then asked, "And how is he now,
Christ?" And he told me, "He is in what is his own," that is, in the two natures, perfect God and perfect man,
"but not in these," that is, he is not in such mortal and corruptible flesh as this, as he was before the crucifixion,
as the apostle Paul says: Even though we knew Christ according to the flesh, that he ate and drank, yet we no longer know him in this way,
that is, although he was formerly clothed in corruptible and coarse flesh, it is no longer so now, for the flesh that the Lord now has is incorruptible.
Again, then, this blessed one says: "As I asked what is the standing and the sitting at the right hand of the Cause":
that is, I asked how the evangelist can say of the Lord that he sat down at the right hand of God,
while Stephen saw him standing at the right hand of Power.
And the angel said, he reports, that the time for this revelation has not yet come either, because of the lack of that fire of incorruption.
That is, because you are still in mortal flesh and have not yet attained incorruption.
All this Father John saw, and he says: Whether I saw it in this earthly flesh, or was caught up out of the flesh and saw it that way, I do not know; God knows.
For the prayer of Daniel reached Nebuchadnezzar and healed him when he had become like a wild ass, and that is why this blessed one says this.
He is speaking of the demon of fornication.
Which of these seven measures receives the crown?
Some say that it is the first, the one who sees the Lord beforehand, but I say that the fifth receives it, the one who says, "I was humbled and the Lord saved me."
By "a mind gone astray" he means the books of the heretics.
Next he speaks of the thirtyfold and the sixtyfold, by which he signifies lay people: married people who have lived in purity with their spouses will gain the thirtyfold.
and to the sixtyfold belong the unmarried and virgins. And to the hundredfold, those who have wholly hated the world and have cleaved to God.
Thus it says that if the flow of tears given by God has run off [?], and the fire of compunction, and they have departed from you because of your great arrogance;
do not cease from prayer until those same God-given tears and that fire of compunction return to you,
for I do not know whether you could find any other such work that procures the remission of sins.
Vision signifies understanding; and by episcopate this father means that the soul should be, like a bishop, master over the passions,
and for this reason he also added and said: "by the mind, the ruler and high priest." Now then, vision of the heart is
a small measure, when a person watches for the passions and fights them; but the episcopate is complete mastery and rule over the passions,
and the ruler is the mind that rightly directs and calms the measure of bodily things.
And the high priest is the mind that purely offers all its thoughts and powers in prayer upon the altar of the holy ones.
For the passionless strive insatiably and forever toward what is desired, and thus they make their perfection unending, for the eternal good things have no end.
He means Abba Tithoes.
He means Paul the apostle.
He means Abba Anthony.
He means John the Short.
He means Abba Ephrem.
By "bridle" is to be understood the fear of God, and reverence, and fasting, and the care of the superior.
And by the two demons he means those of pride and gluttony; for where there is fasting and humility, there the passions have no power.
